subject: Climate & Environment
title: Tidal and Wave Energy
description: Learn Tidal and Wave Energy in one minute.

hook.text: The ocean never stops moving. Tides rise and fall twice a day like clockwork.

buildup.text: Tidal turbines sit underwater and spin as currents flow past, like submerged windmills.

discovery.text: Wave energy devices bob on the surface, converting the up-and-down motion to electricity.

twist.text: The ocean holds enormous energy, but salt water corrodes everything it touches.

climax.text: Tidal power is ultra-predictable — we know tide times centuries in advance.

punchline.text: The most reliable renewable runs on the gravity of the Moon.

quiz.question: What makes tidal energy more predictable than wind or solar?
options: Tides follow a precise gravitational schedule

details.summary: Tidal energy harnesses the predictable rise and fall of ocean tides, while wave energy captures the motion of surface waves. Both offer highly predictable power, but the technologies remain expensive and are at relatively early stages of commercial deployment compared to wind and solar.
details.whyItMatters: Unlike solar and wind, tidal energy is fully predictable years in advance. If costs fall, marine energy could fill a valuable niche in renewable electricity supply.
takeaways: Tidal power is predictable decades in advance
Wave energy captures surface wave motion for electricity
Both technologies are still relatively expensive

faq.question: How does a tidal barrage generate electricity?
faq.answer: A barrage is a dam across a tidal estuary. As the tide rises and falls, water flows through turbines embedded in the barrage. The La Rance plant in France has operated since 1966 and generates about 540 gigawatt-hours per year.

faq.question: Why hasn't wave energy taken off commercially?
faq.answer: Ocean waves are powerful but highly variable and corrosive. Devices must survive storms while operating efficiently in calmer conditions. High maintenance costs and difficulty transmitting power from remote marine locations have slowed commercial adoption.
